section.title: The Righteous and the Wicked
section.sectionRationale: Part of the Hezekiah collection, 25:1 to 29:27, this chapter repeatedly contrasts the boldness of the righteous with the flight of the wicked, the wisdom of keeping the law with the folly of forsaking it, and the futility of self-trust with the safety of walking in wisdom, pressing hard on confession, generosity, and the true source of national stability.
section.thesis: The righteous are as bold as a lion because they keep the law and trust the LORD, while the wicked flee even when no one pursues, since concealed sin never prospers but confessed and forsaken sin finds mercy, and a land is only as stable as its leaders' understanding and justice.
section.frameNote: Four clusters: the bold righteous and the fleeing wicked; keeping the law versus oppressing the poor; confession, generosity, and the danger of hasty wealth; self-trust versus walking in wisdom, and the wicked in power.

units.label: The bold righteous, the fleeing wicked

verses.text: The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are as bold as a lion.
A land in rebellion has many rulers, but a man of understanding and knowledge maintains order.
A destitute leader who oppresses the poor is like a driving rain that leaves no food.
Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep the law resist them.
Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD comprehend fully.

units.label: Keeping the law, oppressing the poor
units.note: the discerning son, the deaf ear

verses.text: Better a poor man who walks with integrity than a rich man whose ways are perverse.
A discerning son keeps the law, but a companion of gluttons disgraces his father.
He who increases his wealth by interest and usury lays it up for one who is kind to the poor.
Whoever turns his ear away from hearing the law, even his prayer is detestable.
He who leads the upright along the path of evil will fall into his own pit, but the blameless will inherit what is good.

units.label: Confession, generosity, and hasty wealth
units.note: he who confesses and renounces will find mercy

verses.text: A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man with discernment sees through him.
When the righteous triumph, there is great glory, but when the wicked rise, men hide themselves.
He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever {{yadah|confesses}} and renounces them will find mercy.
Blessed is the man who is always reverent, but he who hardens his heart falls into trouble.
Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a helpless people.
A leader who lacks judgment is also a great oppressor, but he who hates dishonest profit will prolong his days.
A man burdened by bloodguilt will flee into the Pit; let no one support him.
He who walks with integrity will be kept safe, but whoever is perverse in his ways will suddenly fall.
The one who works his land will have plenty of food, but whoever chases fantasies will have his fill of poverty.
A faithful man will abound with blessings, but one eager to be rich will not go unpunished.

units.label: Self-trust and the wicked in power
units.note: he who walks in wisdom will be safe

verses.text: To show partiality is not good, yet a man will do wrong for a piece of bread.
A stingy man hastens after wealth and does not know that poverty awaits him.
He who rebukes a man will later find more favor than one who flatters with his tongue.
He who robs his father or mother, saying, "It is not wrong," is a companion to the man who destroys.
A greedy man stirs up strife, but he who trusts in the LORD will prosper.
He who trusts in himself is a fool, but one who walks in {{chokmah|wisdom}} will be safe.
Whoever gives to the poor will not be in need, but he who hides his eyes will receive many curses.
When the wicked come to power, people hide themselves; but when they perish, the righteous flourish.

yadah.gloss: To confess, acknowledge, give thanks. Verse 13 pairs this confessing with forsaking sin as the path to mercy, contrasted with concealing sin, which never prospers, the same root used for confession of sin throughout Israel's worship and later echoed in 1 John 1:9.

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom, the skill of living rightly before God. Verse 26 contrasts trusting oneself, called folly, with walking in this wisdom, called safety, showing that true wisdom is inseparable from humility and dependence rather than self-reliant confidence.

basic.context: This chapter draws sharp lines between the righteous and the wicked in nearly every verse: the bold lion versus the fleeing coward, the discerning son versus the disgraceful companion of gluttons, the one who confesses sin and finds mercy versus the one who conceals it and never prospers. It closes by insisting that trusting in oneself is folly, while walking in wisdom, and trusting the LORD, is safety.
basic.hermeneutics: These proverbs describe patterns of moral cause and effect under God's ordered world, not mechanical guarantees for every individual case. The chapter's repeated concern for national leadership, verses 2, 15, 16, and 28, shows these are not merely private virtues but matters with real consequences for whole communities under good or bad rulers.
basic.originalLanguages: Yadah, to confess or acknowledge, verse 13, names the honest, verbal admission of sin that, paired with actually forsaking it, opens the door to mercy, unlike concealment, which guarantees failure to prosper. Chokmah, wisdom, verse 26, is set directly against self-trust, teaching that true wisdom always involves looking outward and upward, never mere confidence in one's own judgment.
basic.typology: Verse 13's promise that the one who confesses and forsakes sin finds mercy anticipates the fuller gospel promise that if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us, 1 John 1:9. The bold righteous, as fearless as a lion, verse 1, foreshadows the confidence believers have in Christ, who has removed condemnation and given boldness before God, Hebrews 4:16.
basic.christ: Verse 13's mercy for the one who confesses and forsakes sin, rather than conceals it, anticipates the gospel's own promise, that if we confess our sins, God who is faithful and just will forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness, 1 John 1:9, a mercy secured fully at the cross. And the bold, lion-like confidence of the righteous, verse 1, points to the confidence believers now have in Christ, who removes condemnation and lets them approach the throne of grace with boldness, Hebrews 4:16, Romans 8:1.
basic.god: God's justice orders both individual and national life; leaders who oppress the poor bring devastation like a driving rain that leaves no food, verse 3, while those who seek the LORD comprehend justice fully, verse 5. He offers real mercy to anyone who confesses and forsakes sin, verse 13, showing that His justice is never separated from His willingness to forgive the truly repentant.
basic.crossReferences: 1 John 1:9 fulfills the mercy promised to the one who confesses sin in verse 13. Hebrews 4:16 echoes the bold confidence of the righteous in verse 1. Romans 8:1 echoes the safety of walking rightly rather than trusting oneself, verse 26. James 5:16 develops the practice of confession commended in verse 13.
basic.oneStory: Proverbs 28 contrasts bold, confessing righteousness with fleeing, concealing wickedness, and insists that trusting the LORD, not oneself, is the path of safety. This whole pattern comes to its fullest expression in Christ, through whom confessed sin finds certain mercy and through whom His people gain the same lion-like boldness before God that this chapter praises.

context.literary:
Proverbs 28 is built as a frame around leadership. Verse 1 opens with the guilty who flee and the innocent who stand, and verse 28 closes with the same two groups: when the wicked rise, people hide, and when they perish, the righteous multiply. In between, verses 2, 3, 12, 15 and 16 keep returning to rulers, so the private virtues in the middle of the chapter are set inside a public frame. The chapter asks what kind of person a society ends up under, and what kind of person you are while you wait.

Unlike the arranged chapters earlier in the book, this one is largely made of antithetic sayings, one line stating a condition and the next its opposite, introduced by the word but. The effect is a series of small doors, each opening on a choice. Several words work as threads that tie the sayings together: law (Torah) in verses 4, 7 and 9, the poor in verses 3, 6, 8, 11, 15 and 27, and trust in verses 1, 25 and 26.

The chapter is not random. Verses 4 to 9 gather around the law, and the sequence moves from those who forsake it, to a son who keeps it, to the ear that will not hear it. Verses 13 and 14 form the spiritual centre: concealment against confession, and the heart that fears against the heart that hardens. Verses 19 and 20 pair labour with fantasy, and verses 22 and 27 pair the grasping eye with the open hand. The closing verses 25 and 26 gather the whole teaching into one verb: trust the LORD, not yourself.
context.historical:
The question of who rules was a live one for the men who copied these sayings. The note at Proverbs 25:1 credits the court of Hezekiah, a king in whose reign the northern kingdom fell, and the reigns in the north before that had been short and violent. A land with many rulers, verse 2, is the memory of dynasties overthrown within a few years, such as the seven days of Zimri in 1 Kings 16:15 to 20, and of Judah's own bad kings.

Verse 8 reflects the economic reality that Israel's law tried to restrain. A fellow Israelite was not to be charged interest on money or food, Exodus 22:25, Leviticus 25:36 and 37, Deuteronomy 23:19, because a loan was meant to relieve need, not to build a fortune. The verse names two terms, interest and increase, which Leviticus 25:36 also pairs as interest and profit. Debt could end in the loss of land and in slavery, which is why Nehemiah would later be so angry at nobles who took interest from their own people, Nehemiah 5:7 to 10.

Verse 17 reflects Israel's treatment of blood. Shed blood polluted the land and could be answered only by the blood of the one who shed it, Numbers 35:33. The man burdened with bloodguilt is not the one who killed by accident, for whom the cities of refuge were provided, Numbers 35:11 to 15, but the deliberate killer, and the verse says the community must not shelter him.

The law in verses 4, 7 and 9 should not be mistaken for a code only for priests. It was the people's covenant, read aloud to the nation, Deuteronomy 31:9 to 13, and a son who kept it is the sort of son this book is trying to raise.
context.canonical:
Verse 1 reaches back to the covenant curses of the Torah. Leviticus 26:17 and 36 describe a people so shaken by judgment that they flee when no one pursues them, and Deuteronomy 28:25 says they will be defeated before their enemies and flee in seven directions. The proverb takes this national curse and shows it at work in a single conscience. A guilty person lives under a small version of it every day.

Verse 13 sits beside the whole biblical teaching on confession. David says in Psalm 32:3 to 5 that silence made his bones waste away and that when he acknowledged his sin God forgave. Psalm 51 is a cry for mercy by someone who has stopped concealing. Daniel 9 and Nehemiah 9 are national confessions. In the New Testament, 1 John 1:9 states the promise in its fullest form, and James 5:16 adds that confession belongs in the community.

Verse 13 leans on the creed of Exodus 34:6 and 7, where the LORD declares Himself compassionate and gracious. The word for mercy in the proverb belongs to the same family as the word for compassion there.

The warnings against the greedy eye, verses 20 and 22, are picked up by Jesus in His teaching on treasure, Matthew 6:19 to 24, and by Paul when he says that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil, 1 Timothy 6:9 and 10. Verse 27's open hand underlies the repeated promise to the generous in Proverbs 19:17 and 2 Corinthians 9:6 to 8, and the leadership theme is carried by Romans 13:1 to 4, where rulers are God's servants for good.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The collectors want a young man to see that character is not hidden. The way a person walks tells you who he is: the bold step of a clear conscience, the glance over the shoulder of a guilty one. Verse 1 is placed first because the editor wants every later saying read in that light. The man who has something to hide is already running, and the man who has nothing to hide is already free.

They also want the reader to take the law seriously as the form wisdom takes in Israel. In this chapter the hearer is not told simply to be clever, he is told to keep the law, to resist those who abandon it, and to remember that a person who refuses to hear it cannot expect God to hear him. Wisdom, in other words, is not a skill that floats free of covenant faithfulness.

Finally, they intend the leader to hear this as a mirror and the follower to hear it as a standard. A ruler who lacks understanding multiplies oppression, and a ruler who hates unjust gain lengthens his days. Even a hearer with no power to rule is asked to watch what he praises and what he tolerates, since verse 4 says that those who forsake the law end by praising the wicked. The first hearers were meant to leave the chapter trusting the LORD, giving freely, confessing quickly, and holding their leaders to account in their hearts.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This chapter describes the usual outworking of choices in God's ordered world, and it commands only a little. Its commands are mostly implied: keep the law, confess and renounce sin, give to the poor, refuse unjust gain, trust the LORD. The promises attached to them are statements of how things generally go, not guarantees for each case. The faithful man abounds with blessings, verse 20, yet the same book knows of righteous people who suffer, and the chapter itself admits that a poor man may be better than a rich one, verse 6.

Care is needed with verse 8 and verse 17. Verse 8 observes that wealth gained by exploiting the needy tends to end in the hands of someone who is kind to the poor. It is not a command to impose that outcome. Verse 17 speaks of a man burdened with bloodguilt and says no one should support him. It describes the logic of the Torah's treatment of murder and does not authorise private vengeance or lend itself to any claim about modern legal systems.

What clearly carries forward is the teaching on confession. The pattern of concealing and then confessing is a description and an invitation. It tells every reader, including those who have failed badly, that there is a way back. It also tells leaders and communities that they will be judged by how they treat the poor.

debates.question: Does verse 1, 'the righteous are as bold as a lion,' promise that genuine faith always produces fearless confidence, so that fear itself signals a lack of righteousness?

views.label: Yes, true righteousness should always manifest as fearless boldness
views.case: The verse's vivid contrast, the wicked flee even without pursuit while the righteous are bold as a lion, could be read as a diagnostic test, implying that persistent fear reveals unrighteousness.

views.label: It describes a general disposition of a clear conscience before God, not an absolute absence of all fear in every believer
views.case: Scripture shows genuinely righteous figures, such as Elijah, 1 Kings 19:3, and even Jesus in Gethsemane, Matthew 26:37-38, experiencing real fear or distress without forfeiting righteousness; the proverb's point is that a clear conscience under God's law removes the guilty dread that drives the wicked to flee without cause, not that righteous people never feel fear in the face of genuine danger.

debates.bearing: Reading the verse as describing the freedom of a clear conscience, rather than an absolute promise of fearlessness, protects believers who struggle with fear or anxiety from false guilt while still honoring the proverb's real point, that guilt and concealed sin produce a fearfulness integrity does not.

debates.question: Does verse 9 mean that God never hears the prayer of a person who struggles with sin?

views.label: God ignores the prayers of anyone who is not obedient
views.case: The verse says that if a man turns his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is detestable. Read strictly, any disobedience seems to cancel the standing of his prayer, and Proverbs 15:8 and 21:27 say something similar about the sacrifice of the wicked.

views.label: It describes a settled, deliberate refusal to hear God's word
views.case: The verb is about turning the ear away, a posture rather than a stumble. The person described has decided the law has no claim on him and then wants God to listen on his terms. This is the hypocrite who wants the benefits of religion without its authority, as the prophets condemn it in Isaiah 1:11 to 17.

views.label: It is a call to repentance as the way into prayer
views.case: Read with verse 13, which promises mercy for the one who confesses and renounces, the verse offers a path: the prayer of a person who turns again to hear is welcome. Jesus' tax collector who beat his breast and prayed for mercy went home justified, Luke 18:13 and 14.

debates.bearing: The proverb does not close the door on sinners who cry for mercy, since verse 13 explicitly opens it. It warns the person who wants God's help while refusing God's word. Believers who stumble can pray at once, and should.

debates.question: What does verse 8 teach about lending at interest, and does it forbid it today?

views.label: It condemns all lending at interest
views.case: The Torah forbade charging a fellow Israelite interest, and some in the church have held, with much of the medieval tradition, that profit from simple lending is itself wrong. The verse reads like an indictment of wealth gained that way.

views.label: It condemns exploiting the needy through interest
views.case: The proverb sets interest and increase against someone who is kind to the poor. The offence is the squeezing of people in need for profit, which Nehemiah 5 and Ezekiel 18:8 and 13 condemn. The Torah itself allowed interest from a foreigner, Deuteronomy 23:20, which suggests a concern for covenant solidarity in need, not a flat ban on all lending.

views.label: It applies the principle, not the ancient form
views.case: The loans of the first hearers were mostly to survive a bad year, not to build a business. Modern credit has different forms, so the underlying principle, do not profit from another's distress, is what is carried over.

debates.bearing: Each reading agrees on the core: wealth built on the distress of the poor is under judgment. Where the readings differ is how to apply the Torah's rules to modern lending, so believers should hold the principle firmly and discuss the details with humility.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 uses a form of the Hebrew root batach, to trust or feel secure, in saying the righteous are as bold as a lion. The same root appears in verse 25 and verse 26, where trusting in the LORD is set against trusting in oneself. The boldness of verse 1 is therefore not temperament but trust: the righteous are confident because they have somewhere to put their weight. A lion does not look over its shoulder, and neither does a man who has placed his security in God.

Verse 2 begins with the word for transgression or rebellion, pesha, the heavy word used of deliberate revolt against a person or a covenant. A land in rebellion has many rulers because rebellion breeds a succession of leaders, none lasting. Verse 4 and verse 13 turn on a single verb, azab, to forsake. Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, verse 4, and the one who confesses forsakes his sins, verse 13. The same word is used for both: you will abandon something, and the question is whether it is the law or your sin.

Verse 13 pairs two verbs. Concealing translates a verb meaning to cover, as one covers a wound or a debt, and it is used in Psalm 32:5 for David's refusal to cover his iniquity. The opposite is yadah, to confess, to throw open and acknowledge, which in its causative stem also means to praise. Confession and praise are close relatives. The promise attached is that such a person will find mercy, from the root of the Hebrew word for womb, rachamim, the felt tenderness of a mother, which Exodus 34:6 attaches to the LORD.

Verse 19 says that the one who chases fantasies will have his fill of poverty. The word for fantasies means empty things, and it appears in the near twin of this saying, Proverbs 12:11, as the thing the foolish chase instead of working the land. The fill of poverty is a deliberate irony, for the man who would not be satisfied with bread is satisfied, at last, with want.

Verse 22 speaks of a man whose eye is evil, as the BSB footnote notes, the Hebrew idiom for stinginess or envy. It is the opposite of the good eye that gives. And in verse 14 the blessed man is the one who always fears, a word for dread or trembling rather than the usual word for reverence, and the BSB note observes that the LORD is not named. The picture is a continual tenderness of conscience, set against a heart that has been made hard and no longer flinches at anything.

typology.type: The one who confesses and renounces, Proverbs 28:13
typology.fulfillment: Verse 13 makes a promise that finds its pattern in the sacrificial system, where a sinner brought an offering and confessed over it, Leviticus 5:5 and 16:21. The escalation in Christ is that the offering is no longer an animal but the Son, and the mercy no longer a temporary covering. Believers have an advocate with the Father, 1 John 2:1, and are cleansed from all unrighteousness, 1 John 1:9. The pattern falls short in one respect. The proverb places the burden on the sinner to confess and forsake, but the gospel declares that Christ has already borne the sin and so makes the confession possible, Romans 5:8.

typology.type: The ruler as lion or bear, Proverbs 28:15
typology.fulfillment: A wicked ruler over a helpless people is likened to a roaring lion or a charging bear, and the Bible gives us the opposite king. The shepherd king David himself fought a lion and a bear to protect a flock, 1 Samuel 17:34 to 36. The prophets promise a king who judges the poor with righteousness and gives justice to the needy, Isaiah 11:4, and Jesus is that king who has authority and is also the shepherd who lays down His life, John 10:11. The type falls short because David and all earthly kings both protected and failed. Only Christ rules as the Lion of Judah who is also the Lamb, Revelation 5:5 and 6.

typology.type: The one who gives to the poor, Proverbs 28:27
typology.fulfillment: Whoever gives to the poor will not be in need. The generosity that the verse asks is perfected in Christ, who though rich became poor for our sakes so that through His poverty we might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9. He fed the hungry, Mark 6:41 to 44, and said that what is done for the least of His brothers is done for Him, Matthew 25:40. The correspondence is real. The pattern falls short because Christ's giving does not come back to Him as a reward for the gift but is a free gift, and the poor are lifted into riches that cannot fail.

typology.type: Walking with integrity and being kept safe, Proverbs 28:18
typology.fulfillment: The one who walks with integrity is kept safe. Jesus alone walked with perfect integrity, being tempted in every way and without sin, Hebrews 4:15, and the safety that follows is not a protection from every harm, since He was crucified, but a deliverance through it. His resurrection stands for those who are in Him. Believers are kept by His power, 1 Peter 1:5, and Jesus says of His sheep that no one can snatch them from His hand, John 10:28. The type falls short because the proverb gives a general pattern and Christ gives a personal promise.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by showing in the clearest possible terms the kind of person and the kind of ruler the world needs, and then by showing the One who is both.

Begin with the king. Verses 2, 3, 12, 15, 16 and 28 are a long examination of rulers, and the verdict is hard. A leader who lacks judgment is a great oppressor, and a wicked ruler is a roaring lion and a charging bear. The Old Testament does not leave this as a complaint. It promises a king who will judge the poor with righteousness, Isaiah 11:4, a son of David whose rule will bring justice, Psalm 72:12 to 14, and Jesus presents Himself as that king. He is the one who puts the little ones first, Mark 10:14, who feeds the hungry, and who is called the Lion of the tribe of Judah and, in the same sentence, the Lamb who was slain, Revelation 5:5 and 6. The ruler who is terrifying to the proud, and gentle to the helpless, is the fulfilment of the hope the chapter creates.

Then the righteous man. Verse 18 says the one who walks with integrity will be kept safe, and verse 6 praises a poor man who walks with integrity. Jesus was both poor and blameless: He had nowhere to lay His head, Luke 9:58, and He was tempted in every way yet without sin, Hebrews 4:15. He is the only person of whom the proverbs about the righteous are fully and unreservedly true. When He faced His accusers He was not a man fleeing though none pursued: He went to meet them, John 18:4. That is the bold lion of verse 1, and His boldness is shared with those who trust Him, Hebrews 4:16.

Then verse 13. The mercy promised to the one who confesses and renounces is not an abstract kindness. It was bought. 'He was pierced for our transgressions,' Isaiah 53:5, and God now shows mercy without ceasing to be just, Romans 3:25 and 26. The tax collector who prayed for mercy, Luke 18:13, went home justified, and the church has always read that scene as the proverb come to life.

A caution is in order. The chapter's sayings about generosity, wealth and rulers are practical and must not be forced into code for Christ. They point to him because they raise a need that only he meets.
study.god:
The God of Proverbs 28 is the one who sees what is hidden. Verse 13 supposes that sin can be concealed from people and not from Him, and that is why the concealer does not prosper: he is working against a Judge who already knows. Psalm 32 gives the experience from inside, a man whose bones wasted away while he kept silent, until he acknowledged his sin. The proverb shows that God's omniscience is meant to be known as a mercy, not only as a threat.

He is just, and His justice is concerned with the poor and with power. Verse 3 describes a leader who oppresses the poor as rain that destroys the crops, and the book says elsewhere that whoever oppresses the poor shows contempt for his Maker, Proverbs 14:31. The God of the chapter is not neutral between rich and poor. He observes, in verse 11, that a poor man can see through a rich man's self conceit, and He prefers an honest poor man to a perverse rich one, verse 6.

He is a God who has a revealed law, which is the shape His wisdom takes for His people. Verse 5 says that those who seek the LORD comprehend fully, which makes knowledge of justice a product of relationship and not of intellect alone. Verse 9 adds the serious corollary: a person who will not listen to God cannot expect God to listen on his terms.

He is merciful. The word for mercy in verse 13 comes from the word for the womb, and the Lord describes Himself in Exodus 34:6 as compassionate and gracious. The mercy comes after the confession, but the confession is possible because of the character of the God to whom it is made. Nobody confesses to a tyrant.

He holds together a moral order and a freedom. The chapter says the righteous are secure and the wicked fall suddenly, verse 18, and it also says trust in the LORD is what secures, verse 25. God's order is not a machine; it is the way a personal Lord governs His world.

For worship, the chapter invites us to stop running. Verse 1 sets the guilty fleeing and the righteous standing, and verse 13 says the way to stand is to confess to the God who is waiting with mercy.

crossReferences.note: The covenant curse behind verse 1: those who survive will have a faintness in their hearts so that even the sound of a windblown leaf will put them to flight, and they will fall when no one pursues. The proverb shows that the curse has an inner form, which any guilty person can recognise.

David describes the cost of keeping silent and the relief of confession. His bones wasted away while he concealed his sin, and when he acknowledged it God forgave the guilt. It is the experience behind the proverb's pairing of concealment and confession in verse 13.

The New Testament fulfilment of verse 13. If we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and to cleanse. John adds the ground that Proverbs does not state, the advocate and atoning sacrifice of 1 John 2:1 and 2.

The LORD's self description as compassionate and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion. The mercy promised in verse 13 is drawn from the same family of words as the compassion in this creed, and rests on the same character.

The near twin of verse 19, which has the fantasy chaser lacking sense. Reading them together shows how the collection circles its main themes, and gives the 'empty things' the one who works the land does not chase.

When Israel spread out its hands in prayer, God said He would hide His eyes and not listen, for their hands were covered with blood. The prophet makes the same point as verse 9, that prayer divorced from obedience is an offence, and then points to the remedy: learn to do right, seek justice, defend the oppressed.

Nehemiah's anger at nobles who were charging interest to their fellow Israelites who had mortgaged their fields to buy grain. It shows verse 8 in practice in the life of the restored community, and how serious Israel's leaders considered it.

Jesus' teaching on treasure on earth and treasure in heaven, and on the good eye and the bad eye, which ends with no one being able to serve two masters. It stands behind verses 20 and 22, which describe the eager to be rich and the man with the evil eye.
Those who want to be rich fall into temptation and ruin, and the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. It makes explicit what verse 20 says, that one eager to be rich will not go unpunished.

Governing authorities are God's servants for good and are to be a terror to wrongdoers. It sets the standard the proverbs of this chapter measure rulers by, and shows why a wicked ruler who oppresses the helpless is a perversion of his appointed role.

The one who sows generously will also reap generously, and God loves a cheerful giver. It carries verse 27 into the life of the church, where giving to the poor is a mark of grace and not only of prudence.

The tax collector who would not lift his eyes but asked for mercy went home justified. It is verse 13 acted out in a single scene: the man conceals nothing, pleads for mercy alone, and is the one who goes home justified before God.

study.oneStory:
Proverbs 28 stands in the long story of a people who hid and a God who came looking. Genesis 3 supplied the first example of verse 13: the man and woman concealed themselves among the trees, and the LORD called, Where are you? Every fugitive in the Bible is a descendant of that scene, and every verse of this chapter that describes flight, hiding or fear belongs to the same story.

The chapter also answers the question the covenant raised. The curse of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 said that a people who abandoned the law would live in dread, and the story of Israel proves it, from the chaos of the Judges, when everyone did what was right in his own eyes, to the revolving crowns of the northern kingdom and the exile. The proverb gives the individual form of this history. It also gives the way out: confession and renunciation, which is the way the prophets keep calling Israel back, Hosea 14:1 and 2.

What it sets up is a king and a people. Israel's kings were meant to shepherd, and the prophets complain that they devoured. Jesus arrives as the king who is the bold righteous man of verse 1 and the generous giver of verse 27, and also as the one who bears the guilt that makes verse 13 true. The church lives in the interval, confessing to a faithful and just God, 1 John 1:9, giving to the poor, and refusing the fear that makes the wicked flee.

The story ends where verse 28 only gestures. When the wicked perish the righteous flourish, and in the new creation there is no more curse, the nations walk by God's light and bring their glory into it, and nothing unclean ever enters, Revelation 21:24 to 27. Nobody there flees without a pursuer. The people of God see His face, and nothing needs to be hidden, Revelation 22:3 and 4.

quiz.q: What does verse 1 say about the wicked and the righteous?

options.text: The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are as bold as a lion.
options.note: Guilt produces groundless fear, while a clear conscience produces confidence.

options.text: Both the wicked and righteous are equally fearful.
options.note: The verse draws a sharp contrast, not an equivalence.

options.text: The righteous flee more often than the wicked.
options.note: This directly reverses the verse's meaning.

options.text: The wicked are bold, while the righteous are fearful.
options.note: This exactly reverses the verse's actual comparison.

quiz.q: According to verse 9, what happens to the prayer of one who turns his ear from hearing the law?

options.text: Even his prayer is detestable.
options.note: Refusing to hear God's instruction corrupts even acts of worship like prayer.

options.text: It is answered more quickly than others.
options.note: This is the opposite of the verse's warning.

options.text: It remains neutral, neither helped nor harmed.
options.note: The verse gives a strong negative judgment, not neutrality.

options.text: It is only slightly less effective than normal.
options.note: The verse's language, 'detestable,' is much stronger than merely 'slightly less effective.'

quiz.q: What does verse 13 promise to the one who confesses and renounces sin?

options.text: He will find mercy, unlike the one who conceals sin and will not prosper.
options.note: Honest confession paired with actually forsaking sin leads to mercy.

options.text: He will still be punished regardless of confession.
options.note: The verse specifically promises mercy for confession joined with forsaking sin.

options.text: Confession alone, without changing behavior, guarantees mercy.
options.note: The verse pairs confession with actually forsaking the sin, not confession alone.

options.text: Concealing sin usually leads to eventual prosperity.
options.note: This is the opposite of what the verse states about concealment.

options.text: He who trusts in himself is a fool, but one who walks in wisdom will be safe.
options.note: True wisdom is set against mere self-confidence.

options.text: Self-trust and wisdom are ultimately the same thing.
options.note: This is the opposite of the sharp contrast the verse draws.

options.text: Trusting oneself is wise as long as one is intelligent.
options.note: The verse calls self-trust foolish regardless of intelligence.

options.text: Walking in wisdom is safe only for the wealthy.
options.note: The verse makes no distinction based on wealth; its point is about self-trust versus wisdom generally.

quiz.q: What does verse 27 say about giving to the poor?

options.text: Whoever gives to the poor will not be in need, but he who hides his eyes will receive many curses.
options.note: Generosity toward the poor is tied to blessing, while willful blindness to need is tied to curse.

options.text: Giving to the poor always leads to personal poverty.
options.note: This is the opposite of the verse's promise.

options.text: Ignoring the poor's needs has no real consequence.
options.note: The verse explicitly names a consequence, curses, for hiding one's eyes.

options.text: Only wealthy people are able to give to the poor meaningfully.
options.note: The verse makes no such qualification about the giver's wealth level.

questions: Verse 1 contrasts the fleeing wicked with the bold righteous. Is there guilt you are carrying right now that is producing groundless fear or restlessness in your life?
Verse 13 promises mercy to the one who confesses and forsakes sin, but no prosperity to the one who conceals it. What sin have you been hiding rather than honestly bringing into the light?
Verse 23 says a rebuke earns more favor in time than flattery. Have you recently received correction poorly, and how might you respond differently next time?
Verse 26 calls self-trust foolish and walking in wisdom safe. Where are you currently relying on your own judgment instead of seeking godly counsel or God's own word?
Verse 27 promises blessing to the generous and curses to those who hide their eyes from need. Whose need have you been avoiding seeing lately?

translationNotes.note: 'A land in rebellion has many rulers' describes political instability producing a rapid succession of leaders, a warning tied to the historical experience of Israel and Judah's turbulent royal history.

'Confesses and renounces' translates two paired Hebrew verbs, acknowledging wrongdoing and actually turning from it, showing that mere verbal admission without change is not the full picture of biblical confession.
'Will flee into the Pit' likely refers to Sheol or the grave, and 'let no one support him' warns against enabling or protecting someone guilty of bloodguilt from just consequence.
